summary.text: A volcanic winter is a drop in global temperatures after a large, sulfur-rich, explosive eruption, when sulfuric acid droplets dim the Sun and make Earth more reflective.
How strong it gets depends mainly on how much SO₂ and H₂S reach the stratosphere, where within about a week they turn into sulfuric acid aerosols.
These aerosols cool the surface for several years, and feedbacks between atmosphere, ice and ocean can keep the climate cool long after they are gone.

facts.label: Aerosols spread
facts.value: Around the eruption's hemisphere in weeks

facts.label: Possible Toba sulfate
facts.value: Four candidate events, 219 to 535 million tonnes

items.prompt: Volcano A blasts out ten times more rock and ash than Volcano B, but B pushes far more SO₂ high into the stratosphere. Which most likely cools the globe more?

options.label: The one with the bigger ash cloud
The one with more sulfur output
Both equally, since size sets cooling
Neither, since eruptions warm the air

items.explain: Cooling depends mainly on the sulfur gas reaching the stratosphere, and eruption size does not track how much SO₂ is released.

items.prompt: Why does the ash from a big explosive eruption usually affect only the nearby area, and only briefly?

options.label: It rises so high it escapes to space
It turns into sulfuric acid droplets
It is too dark to block any sunlight
Most of it falls to the ground in weeks

items.explain: Most volcanic ash settles out within a few weeks, so its effect stays local and short; it is the sulfur gas that lingers.

items.prompt: An eruption's SO₂ stays in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the troposphere, instead of reaching higher. What happens to the acid droplets that form?

options.label: Rain clears them out within days
They linger for several years
They circle the whole planet
They harden into volcanic ash

items.explain: In the troposphere the droplets last only a few days, because precipitation removes them efficiently.

items.prompt: Volcanic aerosols high in the stratosphere cool the ground below. What do they do to the stratosphere itself?

options.label: Cool it, by blocking heat from below
Leave its temperature unchanged
Warm it, by absorbing Earth's heat
Clear it, by pushing other gases out

items.explain: The aerosols reflect sunlight, cooling the surface, while absorbing radiation from Earth, which warms the stratosphere for several years.

items.prompt: An eruption's haze cools the planet, lowering the snowline and letting sea ice spread. Why can the chill outlast the haze?

options.label: The spreading ice releases more sulfur gas
Brighter ice and colder seas feed more growth
The ash keeps blocking sunlight for decades
The volcano keeps erupting at the same rate

items.explain: Cooler oceans and a more reflective surface reinforce the spread of ice, a positive feedback that can keep the cooling going for centuries or longer.

items.prompt: A vast outpouring of volcanic rock covers a region. How could it cool Earth over millions of years?

options.label: Its dust blocks sunlight for millions of years
Its heat drives clouds that shade the planet
Its weight pushes the land into colder air
Its weathering pulls CO₂ out of the air

items.explain: Weathered silicate minerals react with CO₂ and water to form carbonates, removing CO₂ from the air and lowering global temperature.
